task: Find recent papers on community vaccination programs in underserved populations and summarize the key findings. Focus on the intervention strategies used and the measured changes in uptake rates.

documents.title: Evaluating Door-to-Door Canvassing for Childhood Immunization in Rural Districts
documents.body:
Title: Evaluating Door-to-Door Canvassing for Childhood Immunization in Rural Districts

Abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of door-to-door health worker visits on childhood immunization coverage in three rural districts of sub-Saharan Africa. Using a cluster-randomized design across 48 villages (N=6,230 households), we compare standard facility-based delivery against a combined model where trained community health workers conduct household visits to identify unvaccinated children and accompany caregivers to immunization points.

Methods: Villages were randomized 1:1 to intervention or control arms. Intervention villages received biweekly visits from community health workers trained in vaccine education, appointment scheduling, and caregiver accompaniment. Control villages retained access to existing facility-based services. The primary outcome was full immunization series completion (DPT-3, measles, OPV-3) by 12 months of age, measured at 18-month follow-up.

Results: Intervention villages achieved 71.4% full series completion compared to 43.8% in control villages (adjusted RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.41-1.88, p<0.001). The largest gains were observed for the third DPT dose, where dropout between first and third dose fell from 34% to 12% in intervention villages. Caregiver-reported barriers shifted from access-related (distance, transport cost) to knowledge-related (understanding of booster timing) over the study period.

Discussion: Door-to-door canvassing by community health workers substantially improved immunization series completion, with the strongest effects on reducing dropout between doses. The intervention cost approximately $4.20 per additional fully-immunized child. These findings support the integration of household-level outreach into routine immunization programs in settings with high geographic barriers to facility access.

Conclusion: Community health worker canvassing is an effective and scalable strategy for reducing immunization dropout in rural settings with limited facility access.

documents.title: Mobile Clinic Deployments and Vaccine Equity: A Three-Year Cohort Study
documents.body:
Title: Mobile Clinic Deployments and Vaccine Equity: A Three-Year Cohort Study

Abstract: Mobile vaccination clinics have been proposed as a strategy to reduce geographic and socioeconomic disparities in immunization coverage. This cohort study followed 14 mobile clinic routes serving peri-urban informal settlements over three years, tracking coverage gains and equity metrics relative to fixed-site facilities.

Methods: We tracked immunization records for 9,847 children under five years across 14 mobile routes and matched fixed-site catchment areas. Mobile clinics operated biweekly, staffed by two nurses and one community liaison officer, offering routine childhood vaccines plus seasonal influenza vaccination for household contacts. Equity was measured using the slope index of inequality (SII) and concentration index (CI) across household wealth quintiles.

Results: Mobile clinic catchment areas achieved 68.2% full immunization by 24 months compared to 54.1% in matched fixed-site areas (p<0.001). The equity gap narrowed significantly: the SII decreased from 28.4 percentage points to 11.7 percentage points in mobile areas (p=0.003), while remaining stable in fixed-site areas (27.1 to 25.3, p=0.41). The concentration index shifted from 0.12 (pro-rich) to 0.04 (near-equal) in mobile areas. Cost per dose delivered was $3.80 via mobile clinic versus $2.10 at fixed sites, but cost per equity-adjusted dose favored mobile delivery when weighting for coverage among the poorest quintile.

Discussion: Mobile clinics reduced both overall coverage gaps and wealth-based disparities. The higher per-dose cost is offset when equity objectives are prioritized. Route optimization using population density mapping reduced fuel costs by 18% in year three. Community liaison officers were critical for trust-building in settlements with prior negative healthcare experiences.

Conclusion: Mobile vaccination clinics effectively reduce immunization inequity in peri-urban informal settlements, with equity gains persisting over three years of operation.

documents.title: SMS Reminder Systems and Vaccination Compliance: A Meta-Analysis
documents.body_clean:
Title: SMS Reminder Systems and Vaccination Compliance: A Meta-Analysis

Abstract: Short message service (SMS) reminders have become widely implemented to improve vaccination appointment attendance. This meta-analysis synthesizes evidence from 23 randomized controlled trials across 11 countries to estimate the pooled effect of SMS reminders on vaccination compliance for both childhood and adult immunization programs.

Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, and Global Health databases through March 2025. Eligible studies were RCTs comparing SMS reminders (alone or combined with other interventions) against standard care for any vaccination schedule. The primary outcome was on-time dose receipt. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled risk ratios. Subgroup analyses examined reminder timing, frequency, personalization, and target population.

Results: Across 23 trials (N=41,208 participants), SMS reminders increased on-time vaccination by 14 percentage points (pooled RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.21-1.44, I-squared=62%). Effect sizes were larger for multi-dose series (RR 1.41) than single-dose vaccines (RR 1.18, interaction p=0.02). Personalized messages addressing the caregiver by name with specific appointment details outperformed generic reminders (RR 1.38 vs 1.22, p=0.04). Reminders sent 3 days before appointments were more effective than day-of reminders (RR 1.36 vs 1.19, p=0.03). The effect was consistent across high-income and low-income settings.

Discussion: SMS reminders produce a modest but consistent improvement in vaccination timeliness. The mechanism likely operates through reducing forgetting rather than addressing structural barriers. This explains why the effect is additive with access interventions (mobile clinics, community health workers) rather than substitutive. Programs should implement personalized reminders with 3-day lead times as a low-cost baseline intervention.

Conclusion: SMS reminders are a cost-effective, scalable complement to facility-based and outreach vaccination programs, with strongest effects on multi-dose series adherence.
